1.open: Think of a time something went differently than you planned, but it turned out better than you expected. What happened?
questions: Paul says, "I thank my God every time I remember you" (v. 3). Who in your life do you feel that way about, and have they ever heard you say so?

Paul is "confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion" (v. 6). What does it mean to you that God finishes what he starts? Where do you feel unfinished right now?
Paul prays that their love would grow "in knowledge and depth of insight" (v. 9). Why might love need wisdom along with warmth? Can you think of a time when love without wisdom caused trouble?

Paul says his circumstances "have actually served to advance the gospel" (v. 12). He means his time in chains. What does it say about Paul that he looks at prison this way? Is that easy or hard for you to do with your own hard seasons?
Some preached Christ "out of envy and rivalry," yet Paul says, "Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice" (vv. 15, 18). What do you make of his response? How would you have reacted in his place?

Paul writes, "to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (v. 21). If you finished that first phrase honestly today, what would you say "to live is"? You do not have to give the answer you think you should.
Paul says they should "conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel" and "stand firm in one spirit" (v. 27). What makes it hard for a group of believers to stay united, and what helps?
Verse 29 says suffering for Christ has been "granted" to them. That is a hard thing to hear. How do you take it, and what questions or doubts does it raise for you?
1.life: Pick one person who has encouraged or helped you in your faith. This week, write or tell them what you are thankful for, the way Paul does in verses 3 to 5.
1.prayer: Thank God that he finishes the work he begins. Ask him to help each person in the group see what matters most to them, and to give them steady hope in whatever hard place they are in.
1.tip: Verse 29 can sound cruel to someone who is hurting, as if God hands out suffering as a gift. Don't rush to defend it. Let people say it troubles them, then point back to the context: Paul is writing to friends facing real opposition, and he is reminding them they are not alone or forgotten, since he is walking the same road.

2.open: Who is someone who made you feel welcome or put you first when they didn't have to?
questions: Paul asks the church to "do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride" (v. 3). Where do you see rivalry or showing off most easily today: at work, at home, in church, online?
Verse 4 says to look "not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others." What is one practical way someone has done this for you?
In verses 6 to 8 Jesus does not hold on to equality with God, but "emptied Himself" and "humbled Himself." What does this passage tell us about what kind of power Jesus chose to use?

Crucifixion was a shameful death, and Paul says Jesus went there willingly (v. 8). Why do you think Paul holds this up as the example for ordinary church life? Christians read what Jesus gave up in verse 7 in different ways, so how does your group understand it?
Verses 9 to 11 say God exalted Jesus so that "every knee should bow." How does it change the way you think about humility to know the story does not end at the cross?

Paul says to "work out your salvation with fear and trembling," and then adds, "it is God who works in you" (vv. 12, 13). Christians balance these two lines differently. What do you hear in them, and where do you feel pulled toward trying harder or toward simply resting?

Paul asks them to do everything "without complaining or arguing" (v. 14). Why is grumbling so easy to slip into, and what might it be covering up? If you honestly find this hard, or find it hard to believe God is at work in you, what would you want to say about that?

Paul commends Epaphroditus, who "nearly died for the work of Christ" (v. 30), and asks the church to "honor men like him" (v. 29). Who in your life quietly serves like this, and how could you honor them?
2.life: Choose one person this week and give up something small for them: your seat, your preference, your time, or the last word. Do it without telling anyone, then notice how it feels.
2.prayer: Thank Jesus for humbling himself for us, and ask God to work in each of you "to will and to act" for his good purpose. Pray for one person in the group who has been serving quietly.
2.tip: Verses 12 and 13 can start a long argument about faith and effort. Say once, plainly, that Christians balance these lines differently, then bring the group back to Paul's point: God is at work in us, so we can live this out without fear.

3.open: What is something you worked really hard for that you were proud of, even if it was small?
questions: Paul lists his background and achievements: a Pharisee, "faultless" in keeping the law (v. 6). If you wrote a short list of what gives you standing in other people's eyes, what would be on it?
Paul says "whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ" (v. 7). What do you think he meant, and what might it have cost him in his own day?
In verse 8 he calls knowing Christ "surpassing excellence." When has your faith felt like knowing a person, and when has it felt more like a list of things to do? Be as honest as you like.
Paul wants a righteousness "from God on the basis of faith" instead of his own (v. 9). Why is it so hard to accept something as a gift rather than earn it?

Christians read verses 4 to 9 a little differently. Some hear Paul giving up earning God's approval by good deeds, others hear him giving up Jewish identity markers like circumcision. Does either reading change how you hear the passage for yourself?
Paul says he has not yet "obtained all this," but he presses on, "forgetting what is behind" (vv. 12 to 13). What from your past, good or bad, do you find hardest to leave behind?
Verse 20 says "our citizenship is in heaven." What difference might that make to how you handle your work, your money, or the news this week?
Paul wrote verses 18 and 19 "even with tears." What does it tell you about Paul that he weeps over people instead of simply condemning them?
3.life: Pick one achievement or label you lean on for your sense of worth. This week, each time it comes to mind, pray a short sentence in your own words, telling God that knowing him is worth more.
3.prayer: Thank God that being right with him is a gift, not a score. Ask him to loosen your grip on status and to help you keep pressing on toward Christ, one step at a time.
3.tip: Verses 2 and 18 to 19 sound harsh, and some people will feel uneasy about the name-calling. Explain that Paul was warning against specific teachers who were burdening new believers, not giving permission to insult people. Then steer the group back to verses 7 to 14, where his main focus is Christ.

4.open: When you were a kid, what was the one thing you could not stop worrying about, and did it ever turn out to matter?
questions: Paul names two women, Euodia and Syntyche, and urges them "to agree with each other in the Lord" (v. 2). Why might he name them in a letter read aloud to the whole church, and what does it tell you about how he saw conflict?
Paul says, "Rejoice in the Lord always" (v. 4), and he is writing from prison. What do you think he means, and how is rejoicing in the Lord different from pretending everything is fine?

Verse 6 says, "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." What do you tend to do first when worry hits, and what would it look like to bring it to God instead?
Verse 7 promises "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding." Be honest: when have you prayed and not felt that peace? What do you make of that?

In verse 8 Paul lists whatever is "true," "lovely" and "admirable" and says to "think on these things." What fills your mind most days, and what is one small way to make room for something on his list?
Paul says, "I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances" (v. 11). Notice he says learned. What do you think helped him learn it, and where do you find contentment hardest right now?

Many people take verse 13, "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength," as a promise of success. In this setting, Paul is talking about facing plenty and hunger alike. How does that change what the verse means for you?
Paul thanks the Philippians for their gifts and calls them "a fragrant offering" to God (v. 18). Who has quietly supported you, and how could you thank someone this week?
4.life: Pick one worry that keeps returning. Each time it comes up this week, stop and tell God about it in a sentence, adding one thing you are thankful for. Then send a short thank you to someone who has supported you.
4.prayer: Thank God that he is near. Bring one worry each to him in silence or aloud, and ask for his peace to guard the hearts of the group.
4.tip: Verses 6 and 7 can sound like a rebuke to anxious people, or like a formula that failed if peace does not come. Say plainly that Paul is inviting, not scolding, and that anxiety is real and often needs more than prayer, such as friends or a doctor. Let quieter members say that peace has felt far away, and do not rush to fix it.
